FeeBee tests response to injected label noise, but it does not validate the absolute Bayes-error estimates or the claimed interpretation of the target quantity.

Several datasets use labels whose relationship to the theoretical model is questionable. For CIFAR/Fashion-MNIST, curated class labels are not clearly iid draws from the same posterior underlying the soft-label corruption. For ICLR peer review, treating final decisions as hard labels and defining the Bayes error as the error probability of an ideal reviewer is conceptually under-supported.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims: synthetic experiments are low-dimensional and tailored to monotone corruptions, real-world tasks are binarized, and there is no comparison to broader Bayes-error estimators when features are available.

Some technical and reporting details need tightening, including assumptions in the noisy-corruption theorem, calibration/evaluation protocol details, bootstrap uncertainty after fitting calibrators, and reproducibility claims; the manuscript says code is available but the visible PDF leaves the URL blank.

Overall, the paper has technically plausible components, but the novelty and evidence are insufficient for a top-tier AI conference, and the practical claims substantially exceed what the theory and experiments establish.
